notes.content:
---
where'd I learned this from: Husserl/The Crisis of European Sciences
type: principle
reviewed?: true
---
The step back of not only trying to study the scientific methods but understanding *where they come from* shows how much of our "default settings" are hidden. [[Husserl]]'s move in [[the-crisis-of-european-sciences|*Crisis*]] isn't just to point at the [[bracket-drifts-into-metaphysics|bracket-drift]] in modern science; it's to trace it historically. Through [[Galileo]], [[Descartes]], the long arc of post-medieval thought... until you can see when the choice was made and what got chosen against.

You can see it well when you look back at the history of thought and notice "ah, I guess things that now seem obvious to me were not so obvious back then"; and that there seems to be a whole multi-era trajectory you have to look into to be able to see it, trace it back to where it came from, and notice how it could and maybe should start moving in a different direction.

That seems to me what Husserl is trying to say. The diagnosis isn't available from inside the [[natural-attitude|natural attitude]]; you have to *historicize* the natural attitude to see it as an attitude at all. What looks like "just how things are" is the deposited residue of a chain of choices, most of them made by people who are now dead and whose reasons we no longer remember.

This is structurally the same gesture as [[situated-perception|situating perception]], except the situating is *temporal* rather than spatial. You don't escape your defaults by pretending to a [[the-view-from-nowhere-as-position|view from nowhere]]; you escape them (partially) by walking back through the trajectory that produced them. Genealogy as un-bracketing.

The move pairs with [[iterating-particular-and-universal-as-method|the iteration]] from the prior note: myself/other, particular/universal, inside/outside, is/ought — and now also *now/then*. The trustworthy picture comes from oscillating across all of these, including across time.

---

type: argument
reviewed?: false
---
[[Husserl]]'s late diagnosis in [[the-crisis-of-european-sciences|*The Crisis of European Sciences*]]: [[Galileo]], [[Descartes]], [[Bacon]], [[Newton]] [[self-conscious-bracketing|self-consciously bracketed]] purposes, qualities, and consciousness to make quantifiable scientific progress possible. Over centuries the bracket hardened into a metaphysical claim — that whatever was bracketed must not really exist. The methodological move drifted into [[ontological-cover|ontological cover]] for what it made invisible.

The lines that resonate: this is the recurring move of every formal apparatus that has trouble admitting what it can't measure. A civilization that has bracketed away purposes and meaning leaves a vacuum. Letting "I can't measure this" slide into "this isn't real."

It's amusing that the method Husserl comes up with himself, this [[epoche]], seems to be itself another bracketing method — putting aside questions like *what is real?* and *is mind separated from matter?* so that you can note properties of consciousness you can't access otherwise: [[intentionality]], [[horizon]], [[temporality-husserl|temporality]].

What is also interesting to me is that he goes on this history detective story and comes up with his (in my eyes) quite incomprehensible solution through science and psychology — which makes me think that, again, he pointed out enough for us to understand we have to course correct (the diagnosis of what's wrong is very compelling) but where exactly we should be getting at (for example this method of the epoché) is so unfamiliar that we can barely grasp it. Even Husserl himself seems to struggle.

A [[edge-of-paradigm-gesture|thinker at the edge of a paradigm gestures past it but lacks the vocabulary their successors will develop]]. It's like Newton late in his life saying things that point toward quantum mechanics — he'd be skipping too many steps for anyone, even himself, to understand what exactly he's getting at. The same way there's no real point in focusing too hard on what Newton would have to say to quantum-like theories, **I struggle to want to engage too much with this epoché theory.** The diagnosis I take. The destination I bracket — fittingly.

---
where'd I learned this from: Erasmus/The Education of a Christian Prince
type: principle
reviewed?: true
---
[[humanism|Humanism]]  treats *the human as such* as a free-standing object of inquiry, against the [[scholastic-merger|scholastic merger]] of philosophy and theology. Doing so it sets up a trap. The universal "human" abstracts away from the particular, and your [[rootedness-not-introspection-against-shaped-preference|rooted, particular life]] is gets hollowed out. So it seems all the time you have to pick a side to you stand on, the universal or the particular?

I do not believe you can't have both. You can conceptualize the universal human and have that rooted in your own experience; one strengthens the other. That I, for example, can from my own specific suffering infer better what general human suffering is, just makes both my own experience and my conceptualization of human suffering richer.

And in any case, "humans in general" IS NOT a real thing. It's a concept, a tool that helps us project what might be real. Just because it's not real doesn't mean it can't generate real consequences.

While the particular can strengthen or give body to the universal, it can also be true that more particulars can take a better picture of the universal, or that I can know that my particular experience as well as my generalization can be wrong, and maybe that's the best tool I've got.

**Iterating through myself/other, particular/universal, inside/outside, is/ought seems to me to generate the picture of the world that I can most trust and be in peace with.**

The position sidesteps both the [[philosophical-perspectivism|perspectivist]] dead end (every view is local, so no view) and the false-neutrality move [[the-aesthetic-attitude-and-scientific-inquiry|Beauvoir critiques]] in scientific objectivity (a view from nowhere). Neither pole is firm ground. The oscillation between them is.

notes.content:
---
type: synthesis
reviewed?: true
---
Many thinkers insist that some seemingly unsolvable condition (the [[the-gap-between-symbols-and-the-real|gap]], the [[ambiguity-of-human-existence|ambiguity]], the [[the-absurd-in-camus|absurd]], the [[the-lack-in-human-existence|lack]]) is not merely tolerable but *generative*: [[Slavoj Žižek|Žižek]] says the gap is the space where critical thinking and [[creativity]] emerge, [[Simone de Beauvoir|Beauvoir]] says the lack is the condition of [[freedom-as-foundation-of-ethics|freedom]], [[Dostoevsky]] says suffering reveals skills and perspectives otherwise inaccessible. But the [[the-crush-as-philosophical-state|crush note]] remembers me the person *inside* the unsolvable condition almost never experiences it as productive.

The crush is the ordinary person's encounter with the gap between [[symbols]] and [[the Real]] (the beloved is unknowable, the outcome undecidable, the condition structurally unresolvable) and what it produces is not critical thinking or creative self-making but overanxious paralysis, [[crystallization-in-love|crystallization]], irrational obsession, etc. The existing synthesis on [[why-steering-into-the-absurdity-requires-what-both-pathologies-destroy|Cioran's prescription]] sharpens the point: the very consciousness required to inhabit the absurd productively is the consciousness that makes it unbearable. Dostoevsky claims suffering reflected on *in a specific way* opens new perspectives, but the qualifier does all the work and neither he nor [[Albert Camus|Camus]] gives a reliable account of how one arrives at that specific way from inside the condition itself. Camus's [[camus-critique-of-philosophical-systems|critique of systems]] is devastating, but his alternative, a new way of being that doesn't require grounding in abstractions, is described from the philosopher's desk, not from the floor of the experience. The unsolvable may indeed be the space where freedom, creativity, and genuine thought become possible, but that possibility seems to be visible primarily in retrospect and from the outside. 

Easier said than done.

---
source: Herman & Chomsky/Manufacturing Consent
type: argument
reviewed?: true
---
[[Edward Herman]] and [[Chomsky]]'s [[the-propaganda-model|propaganda model]] in *Manufacturing Consent*: by construction capitalism will make it so that scaling up and being able to reach more people, instead of giving power to those same people, actually concentrates power on the ones reaching out — since they become able to more easily [[positive-power-vs-negative-power|shape what people want]] rather than the opposite. So big corporations become this giant subtle propaganda machine.

This begs the question how to know "[[what-you-actually-want|what you actually want]]" and avoid this [[ghost-like-influence|ghost-like influence]], and how subtle this influence will become as technology moves forward.

I think this involves a level of [[detachment-from-the-media|detachment from the media]], the movement of absorbing, stopping, looking inside yourself and around yourself and acting in the world while actively at least trying to think for yourself. This will not be a filter for everything, but it's the one actionable thing at an individual level. Then at a government-like-level the ethics of media also can be thought about and put into law with the consent of the people — again bound to fail at some level because of the residual influence, but a necessary push back to be able to even understand where the [[seeing-the-puppet-strings|puppet strings]] are.

Both moves are recursive: the tool you'd use to escape is the one the apparatus has been working on. But looking inside yourself, as well as I guess your immediate surroundings, is not a move of "fixing" the media influence, but of strengthening your [[rootedness]] which is in a way what media is "attacking" on you and what makes the influence easier to get. This is about, yeah, for example, still reading the news and knowing what's happening in the world, but being also able to step out, absorb the information, compare it with things you have lived and can see around you, [[trusted-locality-as-epistemic-check|discussing it with others around you that you trust]], deciding what values are generated both from having read the news and living your own life and acting accordingly.

The Not-Yet is [[Ernst Bloch]]'s term for the domain of unrealized possibilities that both human [[consciousness]] and the world itself are perpetually oriented toward. It is the horizon of what *could be* but has not yet come into being.

For Bloch, the Not-Yet is a real dimension of reality. The world itself is always incomplete, always in a state of becoming.

"Even a stone is becoming world." 

This means the Not-Yet is not only subjective (what I imagine could happen) but also objective (what the material conditions of the world are tending toward). [[Anticipatory-consciousness|Anticipatory consciousness]] is the human side of this, but the world has its own latent tendencies as well.

The Not-Yet connects to Bloch's other concepts. The [[darkness-of-the-lived-moment]] exists precisely because each moment is partially constituted by not-yet-realized possibilities. [[Art-as-wish-landscape|Art]] encodes our orientation toward the Not-Yet. And [[cynicism-as-philosophical-suicide-in-bloch|cynicism]] is dangerous because it cuts us off from the Not-Yet entirely, locking us into the present.

The novel's final act is a sequence of purchase orders. Candide buys Cacambo's freedom, then Pangloss's and the Baron's from the galley, then Cunegonde's and the old woman's. Each transaction negotiatiated with a different intermediary: Turkish skipper, Levantine captain, Jewish diamond buyers. Freedom is a commodity with fluctuating market prices.

The old woman's autobiography traces the same mechanism across the Mediterranean: sold six times in a single paragraph, her passage through owners compressed into a single sentence of transactions. The syntax is dehumanizing (a grammatical object passed between verbs). The slave economy requires no central authority; it operates through distributed market logic spanning the Mediterranean, Ottoman Empire, and European continent.

Voltaire constructs a world in which the distinction between slavery and freedom is economic.

Resembles [[commodification]] and [[Marx]]'s critique of bourgeois freedom as merely formal. Free in law, unfree in material reality.

Universidade de Coimbra decides that burning people alive is "an infallible secret to hinder the earth from quaking." The earthquake returns the same day. Voltaire constructs a world where the state's response to natural disaster is ritualized human sacrifice, endorsed by a credentialed institution. It is not mob violence but bureaucratic, ceremonial, university-sanctioned killing. The earthquake treated as a policy problem with a theological solution, so to say.

Auto-da-fé has all the trappings of legitimate governance: expert recommendation (the university), formal procedure (the ceremony), graded sentencing (the decorated san-benitos), and public spectacle (the refreshments between Mass and execution). Every component mimics rational administration. 

Auto-da-fé is the chapter's refutation. But Voltaire implies that the failure changes nothing since the institution's authority does not depend on its rituals working, only on its power to perform them.

Similar to [[the-procedure-fetish|the procedure fetish]]: the tendency of institutions to value process over outcomes, so that the ritual becomes self-justifying regardless of its effects. Yuck.

Rogojin's desire shares territory with [[Stendhal]]'s [[crystallization-in-love|crystallization]] (his imagination transforms a the real person into an idealized object) but pushes further into pathology. 

Also, Rogojin never expresses concern for Nastasia's wellbeing; his passion manifests entirely as a desire for access, through gifts, through money, through proximity.

[[myshkin-as-holy-fool|Prince Myshkin]] offers [[nastasia-philipovnas-transformation|Nastasia Philipovna]] everything: marriage, respect, refusal to judge her past, a fortune. 

"You have suffered, you have passed through hell and emerged pure, and that is very much." 

She knows it's genuine.
"No one has ever spoken to me like that before".
She confesses she has dreamed of exactly such a person for five years, and yet she refuses him. 

"You thought I should accept this good child's invitation to ruin him?" She chooses [[rogojin-as-passion-incarnate|Rogojin]] instead: a man she does not love, whose company she knows is dangerous. She does it to punish herself rather than contaminating someone she recognizes as good.
She is trapped in [[shame-internalized-as-identity|internalized shame]]. Accepting love feels like a betrayal of one's own self-knowledge. 

If you believe yourself damaged, then the person offering rescue must be either deceived (in which case accepting would be exploitation) or deluded (in which case you would destroy them). 

Nastasia's refusal is not exactly modesty. More of a stubborn and tragic logic: she has absorbed the world's verdict on her so completely that she can only act in accordance with it. This related to the clinical concept of [[negative therapeutic reaction]] in [[psychoanalysis]] (patients worsen precisely when treatment succeeds, because improvement contradicts their core belief). 

The prince offers her a story in which she is innocent; while she cannot live in a story she does not believe in.

A Christian duality. What is *sacred*? What is *profane*? 
*This* world is the realm of the profane, a fallen place in need of saving. The sacred is transcendent and separate; the profane is where we live in.

This dualistic structure runs parallel to other christian binaries: good and evil, being and non-being. They make believe that the divine is fundamentally elsewhere, and the task of the religious person is to bridge the gap. Through belief, through moral conduct, through grace. The world itself is not the locus of the sacred but an obstacle or testing ground on the path to it.

[[Friedrich Schelling]] argued that this dualism may not be permanent. In his vision of the coming [[schelling-non-dualistic-christianity|Age of John]], the distinction between sacred and profane would dissolve by recognizing that they co-constitute each other, much like the [[duck-rabbit-as-metaphor-for-experiential-framing|duck and rabbit]]. The [[kyoto-school-project-overview|Kyoto School]], drawing on [[Zen Buddhism]] and [[Sunyata]], would go further still, arguing that this dissolution is not a future hope but an immanent reality available right now through practice.

In Chapter V of [[the-idiot|The Idiot]], [[myshkin-as-holy-fool|Prince Myshkin]] describes his Swiss convalescence as a period of increasing happiness. Not caused by events. Caused by attention. 

"Every day became dearer and more precious to me, and the longer I stayed, the dearer became the time to me." 

A donkey braying in the Basel market breaks his post-seizure torpor. A waterfall, a mountain, a ruined castle. None of it particularly extraordinary, yet wonderful because he is present to them. 

"You can be happy? Then how can you say you did not learn to see? I should think you could teach us to see!" (Aglaya)

The chapter frames happiness as a skill of perception, something closer to a practice than a feeling.

Similar to [[David Foster Wallace]]'s [[this-is-water-overview|"This Is Water"]] argument that the real value of education is the choice of what to pay attention to, and with [[Simone Weil]]'s concept of [[attention]] as the rarest and purest form of generosity. 
It also connects to [[contemplative traditions]] like [[Zen Buddhism]], [[Christian mysticism]], the [[Stoic]] practice of [[prosoche]] (attention). 

But in The Idiot there's a specific clinical context: Myshkin's heightened perception is partly a product of epilepsy and illness.
A sort of spiritual attainment by (neurological) accident.

[[G.E. Moore]]'s *Principia Ethica* (1903) makes three claims. 

First, "good" names a simple, indefinable, non-natural property (not just meaning something is "pleasant" or "conducive to survival") knowable only by [[intuition|moral intuition]]. 

Second, an action is right if it produces more good than any available alternative, making Moore a [[utilitarianism|utilitarian]]. 

Third, the greatest goods are personal affections (friendship, love, intimate connection) and aesthetic enjoyments, this is declared "the ultimate and fundamental truth of Moral Philosophy." 

MacIntyre notes these claims are logically independent: one could hold any without the others. He also notes that the first is plainly false, the others highly controversial, and the arguments often defective. Yet figures like [[John Maynard Keynes]], [[Lytton Strachey]], and [[Virginia Woolf]] treated the book as a revolution. 

[[bloomsbury-and-moores-ethics|Why they did so]] (and [[three-failures-of-emotivism-as-meaning-theory|what happened when Moore's framework collapsed]]) leads us to [[emotivism-as-response-to-intuitionism|how emotivism arose]].

The novel seems to argue that optimism and pessimism are not opposites but twins with the same flaw.

Pangloss claims all is for the best; 
Martin claims a malignant being governs the world. 
Candide and Martin debate for fifteen days at sea and reach no conclusion. 

Voltaire positions both frameworks as [[unfalsifiability|unfalsifiable]] and therefore useless: optimism ignores evidence of evil, pessimism ignores evidence of good, and neither helps anyone do anything.

Martin has a different predictive power. He wins every wager about human unhappiness, but no capacity for action or consolation. 

Pangloss's doctrine at least permits activity (however misguided). Martin's worldview counsels only observation and confirmed expectation. 

His "I have lived" sounds like authority but may also be surrender. 

Both men arrive at the garden: Pangloss still asserting what he no longer believes, Martin stopping dispute out of exhaustion rather than insight.

The Dervish slams his door on Pangloss's theological question. The Turkish farmer offers no theory. The garden replaces philosophical debate with manual activity, not because the questions are unimportant but because the debating mode itself is sterile.

This connects to [[Camus]]'s parallel rejection of both [[philosophical-suicide|philosophical suicide]] (systems that deny the absurd) and actual nihilism, proposing [[revolt-against-the-absurd|revolt]] as a third path. It also resonates with [[pragmatism]] in the [[William James]] tradition: the value of a belief measured by its consequences for action rather than its correspondence to reality.

[[MacIntyre]] tries to rescue [[emotivism-as-theory-of-meaning|emotivism]] by recasting it. Even if he believes the *meaning* of "This is good" is not only equivalent to "I approve of this; do so as well," it might still be the case that in *using* such sentences, speakers are in fact doing nothing other than expressing feelings and attempting to manipulate others' attitudes. 

If this is true, meaning and use would be discrepant. Moral language still wears the costume of objectivity, even when it is functioning as preference and pressure. The speaker might sincerely believe they are appealing to impersonal criteria while all they are actually doing is expressing preference in a manipulative way. 

This reinterpretation transforms emotivism from a universal thesis about moral language into an empirical, historically specific claim: in cultures that have lost genuine access to objective moral standards, moral language persists in form but functions emotivistically in practice. 

It becomes, as he puts it, "a cogent theory of use rather than a false theory of meaning," connected to a specific stage in moral development (or decline).

[[Alasdair MacIntyre]] argues that when [[moral discourse]] becomes [[emotivism-as-cultural-condition|emotivist]] (when rational argument can no longer settle moral questions) certain social roles start
gaining influence. Stephen West mentions three: the manager, the therapist, and the protester.

**The manager** translates moral conflicts into the technical language of efficiency and process. Their posture is explicitly value-neutral. They never question what the operation is for or whether it is worth pursuing. They are not wonderers. The manager's art is converting questions about what matters into questions about what works, and this skill becomes valuable when nobody can rationally settle questions about ends.

**The therapist** does for personal life what the manager does for the workplace. The content of therapy becomes self-management and coping rather than questioning, for example, whether the client's entire conception of the good life is worth pursuing. Fundamental issues of how to live get reframed as individual maladies to be managed.

**The protester** make no pretense of value-neutrality. But in a world where persuasion through argument feels useless, public mobilization of a moral position through judgement, visibility, and social pressure becomes an effective tools.

All three characters are, for MacIntyre, natural adaptations to a world that has lost the capacity for genuine [[moral deliberation]].

[[Stendhal on Love|Stendhal's]] framework of [[second-crystallization]] (where a mixture of hope and deprivation cements attachment) illuminates the cruelty of love bombing. When someone overwhelms another person with affection at the start of a relationship and then withdraws it, they generate exactly the emotional cocktail Stendhal describes.

The initial flood of affection can sustain hope for months or years, even as the relationship becomes neglectful or painful. The person remains tethered to the image of what was offered in the beginning and clings to it long after the reality has decayed. The mechanism is the same one that makes crushes so powerful but weaponized, whether consciously or not.

[[Esther Perel]] makes a related observation that often when someone leaves a partner for an affair, the new relationship fails. Part of what made the affair partner so alluring was that they occupied the precise intersection of anxiety and hope. Once they become a stable, available partner, the attraction dissipates.

So what we call love is sometimes more entangled with the *structure* of desire than with the person who happens to occupy it.

The *vereveningsfonds* (equalizing fund) is Amsterdam's primary mechanism for funding affordable housing construction. Because the municipal government owns most of the city's land, it can charge companies and developers for land use. Revenue from expensive, profitable projects flows into the fund, which then subsidizes land for rent-controlled construction. It replicates at the city level what the national government once did with direct subsidies: extract [[land rent]] from high-value uses and redirect it toward affordable housing.

For years, much of this revenue came from the Amsterdam's business district. But the district is now full, meaning the primary engine of the fund has stalled. Politicians have also been moving money from the fund into the general budget for other purposes(?)

The result is that the equalizing fund is effectively empty. The forecast is that if Amsterdam continues as-is, it will be unable to establish any loss-making projects for the next 10 to 15 years, meaning it won't be able to build affordable housing.

Free association: instead of being forced to participate in the society you happen to be born into, the only communities you belong to are ones you voluntarily choose. These are groups of like-minded people with similar goals, where your cooperation genuinely benefits you and their cooperation genuinely benefits them.
What anarchists call [[solidarity]].

This principle challenges the default assumption that membership in a nation-state, or submission to a particular employer or institution, should be compulsory. If a group stops serving your interests, you should have the [[liberty]] to leave and join another community at any time.

This voluntary structure serves as a built-in check on [[power]]. Any individual who believes a group has been corrupted (by drift from its original purpose) retains the freedom to exit (bye bye job). 

Communities must then continually earn the participation of their members rather than relying on coercion or the inability to leave. This is the social building block upon which the larger [[decentralized-federated-network]] is constructed.

[[Simone de Beauvoir]] argues that [[the-adventurer]] ultimately fails because they deny one side of a fundamental duality: the fact that you are simultaneously an individual with personal projects *and* a member of society at large. The adventurer lives as though their life is self-contained. They create meaning, work on projects, and when they die, those projects die with them. 

BUT!

The adventurer stands on the shoulders of giants: the range of choices available to them exists only because people in the past willed their freedom (see [[freedom-depends-on-others-freedom]]). 

Countless people in the present go to work every day, sustaining the conditions that make the adventurer's projects possible. 

The effects of anyone's projects extend beyond their death. Your [[freedom-outlives-the-individual|freedom lives on]], planting seeds for the next generation. 

The adventurer's self-contained picture is just not real. And it is within this "only willing my own freedom" attitude, Beauvoir warns, that most tyrannies emerge.

[[Jacques Lacan|Lacan]] observes that for many people, the primary aim in love is not to love but to *be desired*. What is sought is an ideal version of oneself reflected, accepted, and affirmed in the eyes of someone admirable. In this configuration, the beloved is less of an end in themselves and more of a mirror in which a flattering self-image can appear.

This overlaps with [[stendhal-on-love|Stendhal's]] concept of [[vain-love]]: the tendency to pursue affection not for the other person's qualities but for the validation their affection would provide. The two thinkers seem to agree that romantic desire often has a hidden reflexive structure. It loops back toward the self even when it appears to be directed outward.

This does not mean love is narcissistic. [[Stendhal on Love|Stendhal]] does not condemn vain love; he simply identifies it as one of the things people call love. 

**If we truly love someone, their love for us will almost inevitably affect the image we have of ourselves.** 

The important point is that genuine admiration and ego gratification can coexist. We can experience both simultaneously, which is part of what makes the "crush" so intense and so confusing.

In their book *Homelessness Is a Housing Problem*, [[Gregg Colburn]] and [[Clayton Page Aldern]] systematically test the standard explanations for why [[homelessness]] varies across American cities. Their idea is to identify whether a commonly cited driver of individual homelessness actually predicts *where* homelessness is prevalent.

Higher [[poverty]] rates? No. Cities with high poverty (Detroit, Miami, Dallas, Cincinnati, Philadelphia) have low rates of homelessness. It is richer cities with low overall poverty that see more homelessness. 

Higher [[unemployment]]? The same inversion is true: homelessness is low where unemployment is high and high where unemployment is low. 

[[Mental illness]]? Homelessness is slightly *less* common in states with the highest rates of serious mental illness. 

[[Drug use]]? A slightly positive relationship, but drug use explains only about 5 percent of the variance between places.

What's left that does predict homelessness? The availability and cost of housing. 

When they test these variables, their previously scattered data points coalesce into clear lines: as rent rises, homelessness rises; as vacancy rates plummet, homelessness rises. 

[[California]] has 12 percent of the nation's population but 30 percent of its homeless population and 50 percent of its unsheltered homeless. The cause is not liberal drug policy or generous social services. It is a [[housing supply]] crisis.

An old woman meditates on why humans "detest existence and yet cling to one's existence". She has observed countless people who curse their lives yet almost none who end them: only "three negroes, four Englishmen, and a German professor." Her conclusion is that the attachment to life is not courage, hope. It is an irrational compulsion, a "ridiculous foible". [[Something that operates below the level of deliberation]].

Voltaire leaves the question genuinely open (?) 
Is the will to live a form of wisdom deeper than any philosophy? 
Or is it a trap that keeps us "caressing the serpent which devours us"? 

Related to [[Schopenhauer]]'s concept of the [[Will]] as a blind force beneath consciousness, or [[Camus]]'s opening question in *The Myth of Sisyphus*: whether life is worth living is the only truly serious philosophical question. 
But where Camus treats the question as one demanding a deliberate answer (revolt, not suicide), Voltaire's old woman suggests the answer has already been given (?)
The body tells us before the question is even posed.

The observation also challenges both Pangloss and Martin. 
Optimism claims life is good; pessimism claims it is terrible. The old woman, I guess, would say who cares?: both persist regardless, and no system can really explain exactly why.

Affliction (*malheur*) is [[simone-weil]]'s term for a state of spiritual malaise, hopelessness, and dehumanization that some people can come to accept as the permanent condition of their existence. Not like ordinary suffering or unhappiness. A deeper condition in which people internalize the belief that they are at best a means to an end, not ends in themselves. They are trapped.

In her [[weil-in-the-factory|firsthand experience in factories]], she witnessed the psychological and spiritual degradation that are born out of labor conditions that prioritize [[quota-over-the-person|production quotas over human dignity]] and render [[thinking-as-antithetical-to-labor|thinking itself impossible]]. This is the affliction.

It appears wherever people are [[people-reduced-to-things|transformed from human beings into things]]/objects, anyone caught in systems of [[force-in-human-events|force]] that reduce persons to resources.

The afflicted are then grouped into collectives that are easier to control, rendered incapable of thinking their way out of the situation, and made to feel grateful for the degraded status they occupy. 

Affliction names not just the suffering itself but the entire psychological traps: the learned helplessness, the abandonment of thought, and the internalized belief that they deserve no better.

[[simone-weil|Weil's]] points out that [[attention-as-sacrament|attention]] (the capacity to truly perceive another person) is what breaks the spell of [[affliction]] (spiritual malaise, hopelessness). [[muskism-as-governing-philosophy|Musk's]] DOGE project arrives at the precise inversion: [[empathy-as-software-exploit|empathy is a bug in Western civilization]] that must be patched.

For Weil, [[force-in-human-events|force]] operates by turning persons into things, and the only counterforce is the moment when someone stops, attends, and sees the person inside the instrument. The [[people-reduced-to-things|salesman who sees you as a commission]] is force operating in the everyday; the [[person-in-a-ditch-metaphor|person who stops for the stranger in a ditch]] is attention interrupting force. 

Attention is costly, it requires [[passive-activity-and-negative-effort|negative effort]], the discipline of emptying oneself rather than projecting.
Attention is also fragile, always at risk of being overwhelmed by the gravitational pull towar...instrumentalization. 
But it is what can make us perceive a person *as* a person rather than as a resource.

Where Weil sees attention to suffering as the highest human capacity, Musk sees it as a vulnerability. A social engineering attack against which rational systems must build defenses. Where Weil insists that [[force-in-human-events|force]] dehumanizes by turning people into instruments, the [[state-as-codebase|state-as-codebase]] *begins* from the premise that people are already data entries whose validity is the only question. The [[doge-data-integration-and-the-surveillance-state|"God View"]] with all taxpayer data unified in a single portal, is an opposite of Weil's attention: where attention requires emptying the self to receive the other, the God View requires total informational capture so that no other can escape classification.

[[byung-chul-han|Han's]] [[psychopolitics|psychopolitics]], as some sort of intermediary, shows that [[positive-power-vs-negative-power|positive power]] works by making domination feel like freedom, and that in the [[achievement-society]] the capacity for genuine encounter with the [[the-other-and-negativity|Other]] has already atrophied and been replaced by [[illusory-engagement-with-difference|narcissistic self-affirmation disguised as engagement]]. 

A society that has already lost the practice of attention does not even experience the declaration that empathy is a bug as monstrous. It experiences it as a frank acknowledgment of what everyone already implicitly accepts: that other people are either useful or they are overhead. Yuck. 
The DOGE architects did not need to *destroy* attention. The [[achievement-society|achievement society]] had already done half the work for them.

[[Simone de Beauvoir]]'s ethical conclusion from [[The Ethics of Ambiguity]] is that we should move in the direction of behaviors that maximize [[freedom]] rather shy away from them (since [[freedom-as-foundation-of-ethics|morality depends on freedom]] and [[moral-obligation-scales-with-freedom|moral responsibility scales with the freedom available]]).

Just as we should not deny one side of the [[ambiguity-of-human-existence|dualities we exist between]] in order to flee from ambiguity, we should not deny our [[condemned-to-be-free|condemnation to freedom]]. Instead, we can recognize freedom as the foundational for being, embrace it, and then **orient our actions toward expanding it**. 

Beauvoir also extends this imperative beyond the individual. To truly maximize your own freedom requires maximizing the freedom of others as well. This social dimension puts her ethics apaart from a purely individualistic [[existentialism]] and connects it to other realms like [[justice]] and [[political philosophy]].

[[the-marie-parable|Marie]] "thought it quite right and fitting" that she was treated as the lowest creature. She accepted abuse from her dying mother "without a word," nursed her tormentor faithfully, and never protested the pastor's public humiliation. 

Even when the [[children-as-moral-compass-in-dostoevsky|children]]'s love transformed her final weeks, she accepted their kindness "as a sort of symbol of pardon for her offence, though she never ceased to consider herself a dreadful sinner." 

Social punishment produces not just external suffering but internal collapse. 
The shame is no longer imposed from outside only.
The victim comes to believe in her own unworthiness. 

[[nastasia-philipovnas-transformation|Nastasia Philipovna]], also oscillates between fierce defiance and self-loathing, as I myself often do. Between [[weaponized-self-destruction|weaponized self-destruction]] and the desperate wish to be told she is "good." 

Similar to what [[trauma psychology]]/[[complex PTSD]] later describe: prolonged victimization produces a characteristic reshaping of identity around the experience of worthlessness. [[Erving Goffman]]'s concept of the [[spoiled identity]] in which stigma becomes the master status through which a person interprets all experience also maps onto Marie. 

[[Myshkin-as-holy-fool|Myshkin]] does not argue Marie out of her shame or try to convince her she is innocent. He just surrounds her with kindness that does not require her to be anything other than what she is. 
Still open if this is sufficient to heal it or merely to makes it bearable.

In 1965, lawyer [[Ralph Nader]] published *Unsafe at Any Speed*, exposing automakers who resisted safety improvements while blaming drivers for rising fatalities. Teams of young activists known as "Nader's Raiders" who pursued government and big business on behalf of consumers, contributing to laws like the [[Clean Water Act]]. As historian [[Paul Sabin]] documents in *Public Citizens*, the reformers were right to focus on government failure (strip mines, oil refineries dumping toxins into low-income communities, coal miners suffering from black lung, etc).

Nader's movement built an arm of [[liberalism]] designed to sue the government itself, creating institutions, laws, and leaders devoted to widening opportunities for litigation, almost exclusively targeting government actions, rather than corporations. As a result, the combined emissions of the six common pollutants dropped roughly 80 percent from 1970 to 2020. 

But the same laws and processes that enabled these victories are now weaponized to halt or slow down [[clean energy]] projects using environmental review.

[[Dostoevsky]] challenges the assumption that being an individual requires being different from everyone else. [[individuality|Individuality]] or [[authenticity]] is not opposition to or separation from one's [[culture]], [[community]], or [[religion]]. If this were true, then following cultural norms or religious practices would by definition be [[life-denial|life-denying]], flattening people into conformity.

To truly be an individual is not to be different from your culture but to be an [[instantiation]] of it. To inhabit your place in the [[relational network of being]], aware of your position, and then to make that culture your own through genuine [[consent]]. 

So, there is a way to [[life-affirmation|affirm life]] by first honestly recognizing where you actually stand in the web of relationships and responsibilities you are part of, and then freely consenting to participate in those roles. 

[[Raskolnikov]] tries to become an individual by breaking away from the network instead of owning his place within it.

[[Raj Chetty]] (economist) and his research team have documented that upward [[economic mobility]] is in structural decline in the United States. A child born into an American household in 1940 had a 92 percent chance of earning more than their parents. A child born in the 1980s (just 40 years later) has just a 50 percent chance.

Chetty found that mobility is a product of place. 
A child born poor in San Jose has three times the likelihood of ending up wealthy as a child born poor in Charlotte. Among children who moved from economically stagnant zip codes to richer neighborhoods, the likelihood of better outcomes improved steadily with every extra year spent in the new city, with the earliest movers faring best. 
This means that access to dynamic cities during childhood has compounding, durable effects on life outcomes.

Chetty's team also found that children who moved to high-innovation areas when young were much more likely to patent inventions as adults and the effect was specific to the local specialty. 
(Innovation, like virtue in [[Alasdair MacIntyre]]'s framework, is transmitted through immersion in a [[shared-practices-as-teleology|community of practice]].)

[[Byung-chul Han]] distinguishes two modes through which [[power]] operates on people. 

[[Negative power]] controls through prohibition and limitation. 
Telling people "No, you can't do that" or "You shouldn't do that." 
This is the dominant form of control in [[disciplinary society]] and in most human societies throughout history. 
It works through force, rules, punishment.

[[Positive power]], by contrast, controls through affirmation and possibility. 
Telling people "You can be whatever you want to be." 
Rather than restricting behavior, it motivates us by presenting an infinite horizon of self-improvement. 

Turns out "can" can be far more effective than "should".
It becomes way more "hands-off" because the subject internalizes the imperative voluntarily. 

Han argues that the social unconscious has switched from "should" to "can," and this switch marks the transition from [[disciplinary society]] to [[achievement-society]].

The genius of positive power is that it is [[freedom-as-form-of-control|control that feels like freedom]]. Much harder to resist or even identify.

A vise grip on how things are,

[[Nietzsche]] saw this coming; the French existentialists ([[Sartre]], [[Simone de Beauvoir]], [[Albert Camus]]) lived through its consequences in Nazi-occupied France.

This transition tells us a story about how the need for group identity and moral certainty is so deep that removing one outlet guarantees another will take its place. Whether that replacement is more or less destructive than what it replaced is questionable.

Different existential thinkers respond differently to the experience of the void.

For [[emil-cioran|Cioran]], the collapse of meaning leaves one with [[nothingness-as-ciorans-central-premise|nothingness]], and the task is not to overcome it but to live on without justification, cultivating a love of absolute uselessness.

[[Albert Camus]] responds with [[revolt-against-the-absurd|revolt]] and [[lucidity-over-meaning|lucidity]]: one must live without illusion, yet refuse resignation.

[[Jean-Paul Sartre]] treats the absence of given meaning as the condition of radical [[freedom]]: human beings must choose, act, and take responsibility for what they become.

[[simone de beauvoir|Simone de Beauvoir]] emphasizes [[ambiguity]] and ethics: freedom is lived in concrete situations with others, so the response to groundlessness must include responsibility toward other freedoms.

[[Fyodor Dostoevsky]] responds to the void not by accepting groundlessness, but by treating it as a spiritual crisis that can only be overcome through faith, suffering, humility, and [[active-love-in-dostoevsky|active love]].

[[slavoj-zizek|Žižek]] treats the void not as a problem to respond to, but as a constitutive lack at the heart of subjectivity and social reality; it was already there to begin with; act from within contradiction.

Amsterdam has one of Europe's worst housing crises despite historically being a world leader in public housing. 

It has a social housing waiting list exceeding a decade, 
average home prices above €600,000, 
the highest median private rents in Europe. 

Nearly 40% of its housing stock is publicly funded affordable housing (comparable to [[Vienna]]) yet the system rewards insiders who secured access early while locking out newcomers and the young.

The crisis is not caused by any single failure but by the interaction of multiple compounding forces: defunded [[woningcorporaties-dutch-housing-associations|housing associations]], [[mortgage-interest-deduction-as-demand-stimulus|mortgage interest deductions]] that inflates prices, [[stacking-requirements-and-construction-cost-crisis|stacking requirements and contruction costs]] that paralyze building, and an [[insider-outsider-dynamic-in-housing|insider/outside dinamic]] that divides the population into protected haves and precarious have-nots. The system combines some of the worst aspects of European [[socialism]] (rigid regulation, long waiting lists) with the worst aspects of [[market economics]] (extractive rents, speculation, wealth inequality).

The point is not "a transition away from combustion would be easy", but "from the perspective of what is physically possible, our current energy system is already obsolete".

 [[acceptance|Acceptance]]: the approach found in [[Stoicism]], many [[Buddhism|Eastern traditions]], and various philosophies of equanimity. The promise is that if we learn to accept what is ultimately out of our control, those painful realities will lose their power over us. [[emil-cioran|Cioran]] was deeply skeptical of it on two fronts.

First, he doubted that anyone actually achieves the radical acceptance they claim. 
We accept death but not the hour of our death, as he put it. 
It is easy to accept an abstract future meteor strike; it is another thing entirely when fire is raining on everything you love, as West put it. 

The [[gap between intellectual acceptance and lived experience in the moment of crisis]] made Cioran suspect that most claims of acceptance were just another [[sophisticated rationalization designed to defuse discomfort]].

Second, even granting full acceptance, Cioran argued it is not enough to sustain a human life. In a meaningless universe, getting off the couch and doing anything beyond eating and sleeping requires moral, aesthetic, religious, social, etc reasons. All of which involve the kinds of intellectually dishonest leaps that acceptance was supposed to transcend. 

Similar to his broader argument in [[nothingness-as-ciorans-central-premise|nothingness]]: you cannot live from acceptance alone because life demands illusions to function.

DOGE's logical endpoint was governance by [[artificial intelligence]].
The state reimagined not as a space of [[deliberation]] but as lines of executable code. 

Several concrete steps moved in this direction. 
At the Department of Veterans Affairs, DOGE deployed an AI script to cancel unnecessary contracts. 
DOGE also used AI to locate "diversity, equity, inclusion" language in government policies. 
DOGE announced the "Doge AI Deregulation Decision Tool," promising to cut 100,000 federal regulations within six months. The tool would automate what its creators called the most time-consuming aspect of deregulation: reviewing comments submitted by American citizens. They boasted that hundreds of thousands of public comments could be analysed by AI almost instantly, claiming a 93% reduction in human labour. The implication was that the part of the regulatory process that constituted [[democratic participation]] (citizens submitting their views) was precisely the part targeted for elimination.

Musk reinforced this technocratic framing by wearing a "tech support" T-shirt to cabinet meetings, presenting his role in apolitical terms. But reducing governance to code execution is itself a political act that replaces contestable human judgment with the apparent neutrality of algorithmic output.

The emotional dynamics that make crushes intense also make them exploitable. As [[Stendhal on Love|Stendhal's]] analysis of [[second-crystallization]] shows, doubt can *increase* attachment. This means someone who knowingly keeps another person suspended between encouragement and rejection may be able to keep them hooked while having no intention of reciprocating. In the wrong hands, a budding crush can be nursed into an obsession.

Like in [[love-bombing-through-stendhals-lens|love bombing]]: the alternation between hope and deprivation is structurally addictive. The person being manipulated does not experience themselves as being used; they experience themselves as passionately in love. The emotional reality feels genuine even when the situation is manufactured.

In connection to [[don-juan-as-instrumentalized-love|Don Juan-type behavior]]: when someone treats others as sources of validation or conquest, they may intuitively exploit these dynamics without even theorizing about them. 
So crushes are not only a source of personal suffering but a site of genuine interpersonal [[ethics|ethical]] risk. Being alert to the possibility of manipulation is not cynicism, it can be appropriate self-awareness.

A common defense of [[government]] is that it mediates between all the conflicting interests that make up a society, and so it is what allows people with differing opinions to coexist. Some anarchists would argue that the government does not mediate; it dominates. It is the entity that holds a gun to your head while passing laws that restrict your freedoms, and will lock you in a concrete cell if you fail to comply with whoever is currently in [[power]]. (Putting it dramatically...)

Like the Romans, conquering everyone in their path, leaving a wasteland behind them, and calling it peace. The anarchist question is whether the we feel now in modern societies is achieved through genuine (democratic) mediation or through temporary bouts of domination by whichever faction effectively controls the state.

An anarchist would argue that versions of "[[liberty]], [[equality]], and fraternity", while being good, fall far short of reality. The gap between stated values and actual practice is a signal of domination rather than genuine cooperation. Still, [[liberty-equality-solidarity|Liberty, equality, and solidarity]] are important to an anarchists but they see them different. The gap between stated values and actual practice is itself evidence that the structure is one of domination rather than genuine cooperation.

In [[the-grand-inquisitor|The Grand Inquisitor]], after the Inquisitor finishes his speech against divine freedom, Jesus says nothing. He stands up, walks over, kisses the Inquisitor on the mouth, and leaves. This is a startling counter-perspective to everything the Inquisitor had argued.

The silence is not evasion or politeness. Jesus does not argue back because argument itself is the problem! It is limited to the [[rational-vs-phenomenological-framing|theoretical-abstract framing]] of events, which is by itself incapable of receiving the kind of response Jesus offers. The kiss is pre-theoretical. It is an act of [[active-love-in-dostoevsky|active love]] that models what the Inquisitor's framework cannot access.

This connects to a broader tradition: [[Heidegger]]'s [[Dasein]] and the immediacy of experience, [[simone-weil]]'s practice of attention, the [[ancient-mystery-religions|mystics]]' self-emptying toward communion with something greater, and [[Keiji Nishitani]]'s critique that Western philosophy has been trapped in the framing of consciousness while neglecting [[Nihility]] and [[Sunyata]]. 

The kiss story is an example of what all these thinkers gesture toward: Here's this dimensions of human existence that cannot be reached through argument alone.

[[Murray Bookchin]] used the term "[[futurism]]" to describe a common strategy for deflecting environmental responsibility: 
we put trust in the belief that some future [[technology]] will save us, so acting now doesn't feel urgent or necessary. 
This argument can be applied to a wide range of crises: no matter how bad things get, the solution is always deferred to a future technical breakthrough. This not only delays action but normalizes the damage. 

As early as the 1970s, Bookchin noted that futurists were already talking about colonizing the Moon or Mars, treating Earth as a giant spaceship, imagining jumping ship as a solution to ecological problems. Talking about how whatever-amplified-versions-of-current-technology would eliminate environmental damage. 

The futurist becomes just another [[conservationist-of-the-status-quo|conservationist of the status quo]] that has given up advocating for social change. 

A [[social-ecology|social ecologist]] asks: we do not even have harmonious communities on our own planet; what makes us think we would have them elsewhere?

[[Simone de Beauvoir]] rejects the idea that perception can ever come from nowhere. Every act of seeing is shaped by a particular perspective, formed by one's body, history, experience, etc.

This means that bias is not simply an obstacle to clear perception. It is part of the condition under which anything becomes intelligible at all. A person cannot step outside themselves and encounter the world as a newborn consciousness.

The real danger is not having biases, but believing one has transcended them. Claims to total [[objectivity]] often conceal the [[perspective]] they pretend to escape.

The essay argues that [[jigsaw-as-moral-villain|Jigsaw]] is best understood not as a [[nihilism|nihilist]] or a liberal reformer, but as a strict patriarch. The tyrannical father figure who believes suffering is love, that harsh discipline saves souls, that obedience and gratitude can be beaten into people. His traps are tests of will, but they are also tests of submission. He is always giving instructions: follow the rules, make your choice, learn your lesson. Free will matters to him, but only within the confines of an ordeal he has already designed.

The rhetoric of care, rehabilitation, and spiritual growth disguises domination. He insists his project is altruistic (awakening rather than punishment, rebirth rather than retribution) yet his methods are plainly sadistic. The supposedly benevolent project of [[justice-retribution-and-rehabilitation|rehabilitation]] justifies even more brutal violence than straightforward revenge would.

It wraps cruelty in the language of love.

Jigsaw does not contradict retributive justice. He is the figure who believes punishment *is* rehabilitation, that pain teaches, and that people deserve whatever happens to them if they fail his test.

For [[Slavoj Žižek]], drawing on [[Jacques Lacan]], there is a gap between what [[symbols]] can explain about reality and what Lacan called [[the Real]]  (the full, unmediated complexity of existence). This gap exists between our constant search for truth and objective truth itself, between whatever meaning we manage to construct in our lives and any universal meaning that might exist. There will always be a *lack*, a *negativity*, at the core of human experience.

This gap is [[seeing-things-as-puzzles-to-be-solved|not a problem to be solved]] but a structural feature of [[subjectivity]]. 

Ideologies are designed to make this gap disappear. Offering people a narrow lens through which the world looks simple and fully explained. The ideology then convinces that what we see through that lens is just *the truth*.

Žižek insists that this **gap is useful**. It is the space within which genuine critical thinking, creativity, and political possibility can emerge. But only if one resists the temptation to close it.

[[Albert Camus]] sees the entire tradition of philosophical system-building as rooted in the avoidance of personal suffering [[nietzsche-suffering-is-not-something-to-be-avoided-just-is]]. Philosophers and religious thinkers encounter [[the-absurd-in-camus|the absurd]] and then create systems of theoretical abstractions or grand unifying narratives to escape that discomfort. Oh, make it make sense! They treat the absurd as a [[seeing-things-as-puzzles-to-be-solved|problem to be solved]] rather than a condition to be inhabited.

The result, Camus argues, is transparently self-serving and ultimately dangerous. These systems promise neat moral justifications that claim to apply to every scenario, but they failed catastrophically when tested against [[fascism]]. [[utilitarianism|Utilitarian]] arguments were too weak to oppose [[Adolf Hitler]]. Fatalism rendered people passive, waiting for the end of history. [[Realism]] bred [[nihilism]], leaving people incapable of action. The philosophers who were supposedly providing moral leadership had created beautiful abstractions and then proved helpless when it mattered most.

The -ism crumbles when reality weathers it. 

So what is the solution? The question itself reveals the problem. Asking for an alternative *system* is asking him to play the same game! To pretend that philosophy can provide justifications for human behavior. That pretense, Camus insists, is more dangerous than having no counter-system at all, because it keeps people believing such justifications are possible. What he wants instead is a [[revolt-against-the-absurd|new way of being]] that doesn't require grounding in abstractions.

[[Friedrich Schelling]] places absolute nothingness, what he calls the *[[Unground]]* or the groundless ground, at the center of his philosophy of religion. This nothingness is not just absence but the conditions that allow existence to unfold into the future. There is no independent existence of people, things, or nature... all of these are part of a dynamic, self-revealing process that is constantly moving toward... something.

Similar to the [[Sunyata|emptiness of Sunyata]] in [[Buddhism]], both point to a groundless ground underlying all things. However, the key difference is that for Schelling, the process has a *direction*: a [[teleology]]. All things participate in a progressive unfolding, and this progression toward something is central to his entire system.

One implication is that human history is really the study of how human consciousness has unfolded as one piece of this universal process. We can never understand the *totality* of absolute nothingness through abstract concepts, but human events and ideas are an access point for studying small pieces of it.

Despite his focus on darkness, [[despair]], and the meaninglessness of existence, [[Emil Cioran]] did not consider [[suicide]] an answer to uncomfortable feelings. His entire philosophical project of "[[steering-into-the-absurdity|steering into the absurdity]] rather than fleeing it" is actually very much life-affirming. His message was to embrace life as well as [[melancholy]], dread, [[failure]], and everything else that comes with (honest) existence.

In that sense, Cioran echoes [[Camus]], who opened *The Myth of Sisyphus* by declaring suicide the only truly serious philosophical problem. They both confronted meaninglessness head-on and both ultimately arrived at reasons to continue living. Camus turned to [[revolt-against-the-absurd|revolt]] and Cioran to full-on engagement with pure absurdity. 

Cioran, regardless of how much winney and doomy he reads, is not a brooding nihilist. Suicide fascinated him as a topic but as a practice it was against everything he stood for.

Human existence is fundamentally ambiguous. 

I'm as much a subject for myself (capable of action, free, conscious, mutating) as I am an object for others (looked at, judged by fixed/visible features, reduced to them).
I'm both [[facticity-and-transcendence|facticity and transcendence]], mind and body.
I'm both what I project for my future and what my past projects onto me.
I am me, I am family, I am nation. 

These dualities do not need to be collapsed, figured out, fixed, [[seeing-things-as-puzzles-to-be-solved|solved]]. Doing so is twisted. Being in that "middle" is part of the landscape of our being. Not doing so is [[tension-between-dualities|uncomfortable]]. The question is: [[how-to-live-in-ambiguity|how can one live well without denying this middle]].

notes.title: how to live in ambiguity
notes.excerpt: Accepting finitude, risk, uncertainty, and responsibility instead of seeking refuge in a system that promises final reassurance. The good life is surely not serene metaphysical peace; it is a life of projects, struggles, and a kind of joy…

where'd I hear about this?:
  - Simone de Beauvoir/The Ethics of Ambiguity
reviewed?: true
---
Accepting finitude, risk, uncertainty, and responsibility instead of seeking refuge in a system that promises final reassurance. 

The good life is surely not serene metaphysical peace; it is a life of projects, struggles, and a kind of joy that exists **through** uncertainty rather than beyond it.

An ethics can be built on ambiguity. But [[camus-against-philosophical-escape|it will not look like an ethics grounded in abstract absolutes]], God, or eternal essences. Those let us evade responsibility and flee the anxiety of ambiguity. 

The basis of ethics is freedom as something lived in situations: evil lies in denying freedom, and ethical action aims to sustain both [[freedom-depends-on-others-freedom|my freedom and others’ freedom]]. 

Ethics therefore requires resisting [[oppression-as-enemy-of-freedom|oppression]] and helping create the material and [[|political conditions]] in which others can act as free beings too. So the foundation is neither certainty nor rule-worship, but a shared, fragile, ongoing practice of liberation.

[[The struggle is never finished]], the future stays open, and action always carries risk. But for [[Simone de Beauvoir]], that is [[ambiguity-as-truth-of-ethics|not a defect in ethics; it is the truth of ethics]]. So her final answer is something like: **yes, one can live well and even happily within ambiguity, provided one gives up the dream of purity, accepts responsibility, and wills a freedom that includes others.**

The aesthetic attitude is the attempt to encounter a work of art in a detached and disinterested way. In the history of [[aesthetics]] and [[philosophy of art]], this often means trying to suspend personal preferences, practical concerns, and prior assumptions in order to see the work "as it is."  
  
This ideal treats aesthetic judgment as something that becomes purer the more one removes bias and subjective involvement. It assumes that beauty can be perceived most clearly by a spectator who approaches the work as a kind of blank slate.  
  
[[Simone de Beauvoir]] treats this ideal with suspicion, especially when it becomes a model for how people relate not just to art but to the world more broadly.

The [[The Aesthetic Attitude|aesthetic attitude]] resembles [[scientific inquiry]]. Both seem to ask a person to suspend bias and approach things "as they are." Both value distance from immediate impulse and distrust purely subjective reaction.

Science, however, tries to manage bias through method, replication, criticism, and shared standards. In that sense, it assumes situated knowers and builds procedures to correct for them.

Beauvoir's critique is about this fantasy about a "view from nowhere." The problem is not disciplined inquiry, but the illusion that one can become a neutral spectator untouched by history or standpoint.

This makes the aesthetic attitude or scientific inquiry, when it hardens into false [[objectivity]], an existential danger. Detachment can become a way of avoiding involvement, commitment, and responsibility.
